title.text: Your two hours: 45 minutes are your own work

objects.text: 45 of the 120 minutes are yours: your numbers, your costs, your decision.

slides.notes: Three parts take most of the time. Twenty-five minutes of ideas on costs, benefits, payback, sensitivity and stop rules. Twenty minutes of worked examples: the Monday sales email at Nile Valley Foods, the customer message workflow from Session 8, and the invoice check. After the break you have forty-five minutes on your own task, in three blocks of fifteen. The last ten minutes are for your decision.

title.text: Three questions from last time

runs.text: 1.  Name three of the five oversight controls for a tool you buy.
2.  On the Vendor Question List, what does a 0 in data and privacy, security, or contract and exit mean?
3.  How many of the 11 planted red flags did the two AI reviews catch, and what did you still have to do?

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_question_2.80.png

objects.text: Answer aloud first. Then we check together.

slides.notes:
Three quick questions from Session 10. Answer aloud first, and then we check together. It is a warm-up to bring last time back.

Question one. Name three of the five oversight controls for a tool you buy. Take a moment.

A good answer is this. Any three of: data location, terms, exit, audit, owner.

Question two. On the Vendor Question List, what does a 0 in data and privacy, security, or contract and exit mean? Say it to yourself first.

A good answer is this. It is a reason to stop. A 0 is a red flag, a refusal or silence.

Question three. How many of the 11 planted red flags did the two AI reviews catch, and what did you still have to do? Think about your own task as you answer.

A good answer is this. Both runs caught all 11. You still check its quotes, send the questions and judge the vendor’s written answers.

If an answer was missing, your own task card or last workbook page has it. Now to today.

slides.notes:
Five words for today. I give the plain meaning of each, and we use every one of them before the end of the session.

Payback. The number of months the monthly net takes to repay the one-off cost.

Loaded hourly cost. Pay plus employer contributions and benefits, divided by hours worked. It is what an hour of staff time costs the company.

Haircut. The share of the benefit you choose not to count, because estimates are rarely exact.

Sensitivity. Trying a low, base and high version of your numbers to see whether the answer changes.

Stop rule. A number written in advance that tells you to stop or revise.

title.text: A business case puts money on your baseline

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_flow_11.90x3.90_1666d4e3.png

objects.text: You hold the first step already. Today you add the money.

slides.notes:
Today’s question is whether a task is worth doing and what would change your mind. A business case takes the baseline you wrote in Session 1 and puts money on both sides: costs, then benefits, then payback, a haircut for risk and stop rules. Why bother?

Gartner forecast in June 2025 that over forty percent of agentic AI projects will be cancelled by the end of 2027, mainly because of rising cost, unclear value and weak risk controls. A short, honest case is your answer to it. Ask me for the reference. Tell me now which number you are least sure of.

slides.notes:
This is the finished task card from Session 1, with the letters that tell you how solid each number is. Ninety minutes a run, four runs a month, so six hours a month. Mistakes in four emails out of ten, and one mistake costs about one hundred and fifty thousand shillings.

Better means a draft in ten minutes and a check in twenty. For the hourly cost, pay of four and a half million plus employer contributions of half a million, over one hundred and sixty hours, is about thirty-one thousand shillings. The workbook rounds it to thirty thousand.

In the workbook, the ten minutes becomes the minutes with the tool, and the twenty is the review. Notice that most numbers are estimates, and that is acceptable if you say so.

slides.notes:
These are the cost lines in the workbook, with the Nile Valley Foods figures. The tool licence is monthly, and the figure is an invented example, so use your own quote. Set-up and data preparation happen once: building it, testing it and tidying the data it reads. Training happens once.

Review time repeats every month, four runs of twenty minutes, and it never goes away, so never set it to zero. Upkeep is the time to fix and update. The total is UGX 480,000 once and UGX 145,000 each month. If you buy or partner, put the vendor’s first-year total in these lines.

title.text:
Benefits: count hours and
errors, and write down the rest

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_bars_7.70x4.80_1a62422d.png
objects.alt: Benefits: count hours and errors, and write down the rest

objects.text: Count hours and errors. Count other benefits at zero.

runs.text: Hours: 4 runs x 80 minutes x UGX 30,000 an hour.
Errors: 4 runs x 40% x 60% removed x UGX 150,000.
Faster replies: write it, count 0.

slides.notes:
Benefits come from your baseline and your plan. Time saved is the runs a month, times the minutes saved before review, times the hourly cost. At Nile Valley Foods that is four runs times eighty minutes, which is 5.3 hours, at UGX 30,000 an hour: UGX 160,000 a month.

The eighty is ninety minutes today less the ten minutes of your own work with the tool. Errors avoided is runs, times the error rate, times the share removed, times the cost of one error: UGX 144,000. The sixty percent removed is a plan, so mark it as an estimate.

Goodwill is real, but I count it at zero unless you can show a number. Benefit of 304,000 less cost of 145,000 leaves a net of UGX 159,000 a month.

title.text:
On plan, the Monday email
pays back in 3.0 months

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_card_7.70x4.80_f2ca4ef3.png
objects.alt: On plan, the Monday email pays back in 3.0 months

objects.text: The haircut shows how much of the benefit can vanish.

runs.text: These are plan numbers.
Positive until about 39% of the benefit fails to appear.
Measure in a pilot before you trust it.

slides.notes:
Here is the result. A monthly net of UGX 159,000. The one-off cost of UGX 480,000 divided by 159,000 is 3.0 months to pay back. Twelve months net of the one-off cost is UGX 1,428,000. Then the haircut: I choose not to count thirty percent of the benefit, and the twelve month net is still UGX 333,600.

The break-even haircut is about thirty-nine percent, which means more than a third of the benefit can fail to appear before the case reaches zero. These are plan numbers, built from estimates. A pilot replaces them with measured numbers.

title.text:
Low, base and high: NVF is positive
in two cases and negative in one

objects.text: A case that is positive in only two of three scenarios needs a stop rule for the low case.

slides.notes:
This is the Sensitivity sheet with the workbook’s default factors. The monthly net is minus UGX 80,980 in the low case, UGX 159,000 in the base case and UGX 270,780 in the high case. In the low case volume is seventy percent, only sixty percent of the saving happens, only forty percent of the errors are removed, and costs are thirty percent higher.

The result is no payback. The haircut shrinks the benefit, and sensitivity changes the assumptions, so I use both. Nile Valley Foods is positive in two of three cases, so I ask what would have to be true in the low case, and I write it as a stop rule.

slides.notes:
What would change my mind?

Write it down now, while you are calm. These are example rules for Nile Valley Foods. Stop if one error reaches a customer or the bank. Revise if review minutes climb above thirty a run. Revise if the twelve month net after the haircut turns negative. Stop if the saving after four weeks is under half the plan.

Scale only after the base case holds for two months. Each rule is a number somebody can check. In Session 12 these become part of your ninety day plan, so choose numbers you can read from your own records.

title.text: The AI found all 8 invoice problems in both runs

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_catch_11.90x4.25_46abb79b.png
objects.alt: The AI found all 8 invoice problems in both runs

objects.text: Claude, a fresh session given only the prompt, 4 November 2026, answer key hidden. Two runs.

slides.notes:
Now a second example, the invoice check. I gave sixty supplier invoices to Claude in two fresh sessions, each given only the prompt, and asked for duplicates, missing purchase order numbers and totals that do not add up. This was Claude on the fourth of November 2026, not ChatGPT or Gemini, with the key hidden.

Both runs found all eight problems and raised no false alarm. On the zero percent VAT invoice, both said they were unsure and told us to ask the supplier. Both said they did the sums without code, which is their own statement. Run two also said dates and PO numbers were in sequence, which is not quite true. I recomputed all sixty rows: the eight are the only problems.

I recomputed each of the eight problems from the invoice file. Two different sums sit in this table. The duplicate invoice is for UGX 13,973,560, which would be paid twice. The two invoices with no purchase order number are for UGX 14,610,760 and UGX 4,307,000, and their amounts are correct: they are held until a purchase order is found, not lost.

slides.notes:
Here is the lesson for your business case. Every check costs time. With the AI route you confirm the eight flags against the invoices, and then you face a choice about the other fifty-one invoices it passed. Both runs said everything else matched, and that was true here, but you only know it if you redo the sums, and a formula does exactly that.

A formula in the sheet checks every row the same way every run, and it flags a missing purchase order or a duplicate. It cannot judge the zero percent VAT, so a person still does that. In your workbook, the formula route has set-up hours and almost no review minutes.

Fill result against baseline, cost and risk. Label planned numbers as plan.
Write the decision you ask for in one sentence.

objects.text: You keep: A one-page summary: result, cost, risk, stop rules and the decision requested.

slides.notes:
The last fifteen minutes of your own work. First write three stop rules, as numbers somebody can check. Then open the Sponsor Briefing. A sponsor is the person who owns the result and asks for the decision. In a small company that may be you, and the page goes to the owner of the business or the board.

Fill it in with your planned numbers and label them as plan. After a pilot you replace them with measured numbers. Write one sentence that says what you want decided. Read it aloud. If it takes more than two minutes, cut it.

title.text: Decision: go to a pilot, revise or stop?

objects.text: What do you decide, and which number decided it?

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_check_0.80.png

objects.text: Go to a pilot
Positive after the haircut and in at least two cases. Start a limited pilot with a review date.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_gear_0.80.png

objects.text: Revise
Positive only in the base case. Fix the weakest number: review time, error cost or price.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_cross_0.80.png

objects.text: Stop
Negative after the haircut and in every case. Keep the workbook and retest when a number changes.
Write the decision and the one number that decided it on the summary page.

slides.notes:
Time to decide. Go to a pilot means the case is positive after the haircut and in at least two of the three cases. Your numbers are still plan numbers, so the next step is a limited pilot with a review date, which gives you measured numbers. Revise means it is positive only in the base case, so fix the weakest number: review time, error cost or the tool price.

Stop means it is negative after the haircut, so keep the workbook and test again when a number changes. A stop with a clear reason also saves money. Write your decision and the one number that decided it.
